title: Luca Guadagnino Confirms ‘American Psycho’ Film Halted, Says No Further Development Planned
body:
Luca Guadagnino has confirmed that his long‑awaited re‑imagining of American Psycho will not move forward, effectively shelving the latest attempt to revive Bret Easton Ellis’s controversial novel for a new generation. The director disclosed the news during a candid interview on Deadline’s Crew Call podcast with producer Anthony D’Alessandro, explaining that a combination of creative disagreements and shifting studio priorities led Lionsgate to pull the plug on the project.

The aborted film would have been the second major cinematic adaptation of the 1991 novel, following the 2000 cult classic starring Christian Bale, which cemented the story’s place in popular culture. This time, the script was penned by Oscar‑winning screenwriter Scott Z. Burns, whose résumé includes the thriller The Giver and the sci‑fi drama Contagion. Burns’ involvement raised expectations that the new version would lean heavily into the novel’s satirical critique of 1980s yuppie excess while updating its tone for contemporary audiences. Guadagnino, known for his lush, character‑driven works such as Call Me By Your Name and Suspiria, was expected to bring a visually striking, psychologically nuanced perspective to the story of Patrick Bateman, the murderous Wall Street executive whose veneer of perfection masks a violent inner life.

Industry insiders suggest that the project’s demise reflects broader challenges in adapting material that straddles horror, dark comedy, and social commentary. While the original film managed to balance these elements, modern sensibilities have grown increasingly attuned to issues of misogyny and violence, prompting studios to tread carefully with content that could be perceived as glorifying a misogynistic anti‑hero. In recent years, other high‑profile adaptations of Ellis’s work, such as The Great American Novel project “Less Than Zero,” have encountered similar hurdles, indicating a cautious approach from financiers when dealing with the author’s provocative themes.

Lionsgate’s decision also appears tied to shifting market dynamics. The streaming boom has altered the calculus for mid‑budget prestige projects, with studios favoring franchise tentpoles or content that can be easily serialized. An auteur‑driven, adult‑oriented thriller like American Psycho might struggle to find a clear distribution pathway, especially given the polarizing nature of its source material. Moreover, the pandemic‑induced production delays and rising costs have made studios more risk‑averse, prompting them to prioritize projects with clearer commercial upside.

For Guadagnino, the setback is likely a disappointment but not necessarily a career‑ending detour. The director has a track record of navigating setbacks and emerging with critically acclaimed work, as demonstrated by his recent foray into television with the limited series We Are Who We Are. In the meantime, the script by Burns remains intact, and it is possible that another director or studio could revive the material under different conditions. The novel’s enduring relevance—its critique of consumer culture, identity performance, and moral vacuity—continues to attract filmmakers seeking to reinterpret its themes for a new era.

Looking ahead, the cancellation underscores the delicate balance between artistic ambition and commercial viability in today’s entertainment landscape. While Guadagnino’s vision for American Psycho will not see the light of day for now, the conversation it sparked highlights the persistent allure of Ellis’s work and the ongoing appetite for bold, boundary‑pushing storytelling. As studios recalibrate their strategies, audiences can expect future attempts to revisit the novel’s dark satire, perhaps in formats better suited to its complex tone—be it limited series, streaming exclusives, or even experimental theatrical releases.
